newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia faces deadline on debt payment to World Bank.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia faces deadline on debt payment to World Bank.

text.p: Prospects for raising reconstruction aid for Bosnia could be damaged if the country fails to pay an $8 million instalment on its external debt by a Friday deadline, World Bank officials said.
Bosnia inherited a two billion dollar share of former Yugoslavia's debt and is currently servicing a consolidated $680 million loan to the World Bank with regular six-month payments.

"This amount was due May 15 and with a 30-day payment period it becomes due tomorrow, but tomorrow is Saturday, so it becomes seriously due today," Rory O'Sullivan, the World Bank's Sarajevo director, said.
Officials from the country's cash-strapped Serb entity emerged after a central government session on Thursday saying they have no funds to pay their $3.8 million share of the $8 million installment.

The Serb entity, which covers half of Bosnia, has received only about two percent of more than a billion dollars in international aid which poured into the country last year because Serb authorities have failed to abide by terms of a peace agreement.
The deadline for payment will expire when bank offices close on Friday in New York, Christine Wallich, director of the World Bank in Bosnia, told reporters.

Wallich said if the debt was not paid on Friday no new projects for Bosnia would be presented to the bank's board of directors and it would not be possible to lend the country money to repay the debt.

Bosnia could also be deprived of World Bank replenishment for liquidity accounts if the debt is not paid in the next 45 days and risks suspension of all disbursements for ongoing reconstruction projects after 60 days of non-payment, she said.

With a fund-raising conference scheduled in Brussels on June 24 and 25, officials fear the debt problem could undermine plans to win pledges for an estimated $1.4 billion needed for reconstruction in 1997.
"There's clearly a certain awkwardness for the World Bank in chairing and sponsoring a donor conference if Bosnia remains in arrears at that time," Wallich said.
"The danger is if the donors see a situation of non-payment of debt, then they could be less forthcoming," O'Sullivan said.
"It creates a feeling of uncertainty," he said.

Wallich said Bosnia had a good payment record since it started external debt service after rejoining the World Bank in April 1996 as one of the successor states of former Yugoslavia. She said she was hopeful the issue would be resolved.
Bosnian government officials were meeting to resolve the problem on Friday and were unavailable for comment.
